content:
DC Studios' body-horror gamble paid off at the box office this weekend. Clayface, the R-rated origin story of the Batman villain, opened at No. 1 in North America, earning $10.4 million on Friday, October 23, from 3,458 theaters — a figure that includes $3.5 million from Thursday night previews — and tracking toward a $24 million to $25 million opening weekend, according to Deadline's box-office reporting.

The film stars Tom Rhys Harries as Matt Hagen, a Hollywood actor whose face is ruined and who turns to a scientist, played by Naomi Ackie, for help — a bargain that makes his situation worse. James Watkins directs from a screenplay by Mike Flanagan and Hossein Amini, from a story by Flanagan. Max Minghella, Eddie Marsan and David Dencik co-star. It is the first R-rated film in DC Studios co-chief James Gunn's DC Universe, rated for strong bloody violence, gore, language, some nudity and brief drug use.

What sets the opening apart is not just the gross but the audience grade. Clayface earned an A- CinemaScore, a rare mark for a horror film. Gunn highlighted the result on Threads, writing: "Really proud of this. Sinners is the only horror movie to have EVER gotten an A Cinemascore." The film also holds roughly a 94 percent audience score on Rotten Tomatoes, with critics in the mid-70s, and praise centered on Harries' lead performance and the film's practical makeup and body-horror effects.

The economics favor DC Studios. The film reportedly cost about $44 million to produce, a fraction of the $170 million spent on Supergirl, which opened to $37.1 million over the summer. Clayface also added $4.3 million internationally on Friday. A24's You Can See Everything follows in second place, projected at $19 million to $20 million in its second weekend after expanding to more than 2,500 screens.

Analysis: A Small Bet That Changes the DC Math

Clayface matters less as a franchise launch than as a proof of concept. DC Studios picked one of its stranger villains — a shape-shifting actor-monster with no built-in mass audience — kept the budget low, leaned into horror instead of superhero spectacle, and let the movie stand on its own rather than serve as setup for the next tentpole. The A- CinemaScore is the number that will echo in studio meetings: horror audiences are notoriously harsh graders, and a grade that high usually means strong word of mouth, which is exactly what a film like this needs heading into the first Saturday Halloween since 2020. If the weekend holds, DC's cheapest path to a hit may turn out to be its weirdest one — and for audiences in Laredo and the Rio Grande Valley, the takeaway is simple: the scariest movie at the multiplex this Halloween weekend is also the one critics and crowds agree on.
